newsitem.title: USA: Multimillionaire du Pont heir sentenced for murder.
newsitem.headline: Multimillionaire du Pont heir sentenced for murder.

text.p: Multimillionaire chemicals heir John du Pont was sentenced on Tuesday to spend 13 to 30 years in prison or a mental health treatment facility for the January 1996 shooting death of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
State Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins pronounced the sentence after a day-long hearing punctuated by emotional testimony from Schultz's relatives and a courtroom apology by du Pont.
"I finally concluded that I was ill...and I wish to apologise to Nancy Schultz and her children," du Pont said, referring to Schultz's widow in speaking publicly for the first time about the killing.
"I am very sorry for what happened, and I wish them all the best in the future," du Pont said in a clear but quiet and expressionless voice.

Du Pont's hair and beard, shaggy and long during his four-week trial, were neatly trimmed. He wore a dark blue sweatsuit of the Foxcatcher Farm athletic teams he sponsored at his suburban Philadelphia estate.
Du Pont, 58, was found guilty but mentally ill in February on a charge of third-degree murder in Schultz's killing.

He is a great-great-grandson of E.I. du Pont, who in 1802 founded the chemical firm that bears his name and that created one of America's largest family fortunes. John du Pont's personal wealth has been estimated at up to $250 million.

Witnesses at his trial said du Pont shot Schultz three times with a .44 calibre handgun outside the wrestler's home on the du Pont estate. The shooting was followed by a 48-hour police standoff before du Pont's capture.

Jenkins said she was departing from state sentencing guidelines of five to 10 years in part because of the impact of the killing on those close to Schultz. But she also said du Pont's mental illness was a mitigating factor.

"The sentence is not a life sentence," she said. Du Pont can be released on parole after serving 13 years unless state corrections officials determine he is a danger to society. He will also be given credit for time served.

Jenkins said the 30-year maximum term of the sentence will ensure that he receives continued treatment under the authority of parole officers even after his release. "As long he lives, his mental illness cannot be ignored," she said.
Jenkins determined on Tuesday that du Pont was "severely mentally disabled" and ordered that he be treated for what a court-appointed psychiatrist said was paranoid schizophrenia.
Du Pont will most likely be confined in a state psychiatric facility until corrections officials determine he is fit to go to prison, attorneys on both sides said.

His longtime attorney, Taras Wochok, told reporters after the sentence was announced, "I'm personally disappointed for him, and my sense is that he will probably be disappointed with the sentence." He said the "greater likelihood" was that du Pont would seek an appeal.
Schultz's widow, Nancy, said: "I'm glad this long, painful journey is over. ... I'm glad that we have closure."
Prosecutor Dennis McAndrews said, "The one relief I have is that John du Pont will not be able to set a toe out of prison until he is older than 70 years old."
